title: Four bat myths we hear on the water
why: Myth vs fact for bat-curious visitors whose hesitation is the bats themselves, not the kayak.
hook_options: Bats in your hair? Let's settle this.
Four things people get wrong about Austin's bats
What the bats actually do when you're under them
caption: Will the bats fly into my hair? Are they here all year? Can a first-timer do this at dusk? And yes, the guano thing. Four myths, four straight answers from Lady Bird Lake. #austinbats #congressavenuebridge #ladybirdlake #austinkayaktours

slides.headline: Four bat myths we hear on the water
slides.body: Guests show up with these every week. The colony doesn't care, but your evening goes better without them.

slides.headline: The bats will fly into your hair
They're hunting bugs, not kayakers
slides.body: The colony streams out to feed on insects over the city. You sit underneath and watch them pass high overhead.

slides.headline: The bats are here all year
They leave with the fall cold fronts
slides.body: Most of the colony heads south by early November and returns in spring. Late-October flights run smaller and later.

slides.headline: Dusk kayaking is for experienced paddlers
Flat water, a guide, a land lesson first
slides.body: Lusell K. called it "perfect for first-time kayakers." The guide paddles with the group the whole way.

slides.headline: Guano happens. Apparently it's lucky.
slides.body: Brittany H. learned that "bat guano feels like rain when it falls on you, and supposedly it's good luck." Wear washable clothes.

slides.headline: Come see what's true for yourself
slides.body: A few weeks of bat season left. Sunset bat tours at austinkayaktours.com.
